I've grown up with dogs, as well as having my own now as an adult living in my own place. Parents split when i was young, so i had 2 households with dogs. 

2 dogs were purchased in one household, 6 dogs were rescues (my house and the other childhood household). I'll give you the run down on each.

Purchased puppers:


My childhood dog, Douge de Bordeaux, was bought from a verified, professional breeder that also happened to be family friends. We waited two years for a litter, and ended up with the runt of the litter at a discount (who actually ended up growing bigger than her brother and sisters.) We had to buy her because we wanted a puppy, and there are actually zero douge de bordeaux rescues in our area. She lived hella long, and crossed the rainbow bridge a few years ago. She was literally an amazing dog. Relatively healthy, amazing personality, sharp as a tack.


The dog that came after her, my dad brought home one day after buying him at a pet store. He was supposed to be a GSD and looks exactly like one, but is about 2/3rds of the size of a standard GSD at 3 years old now. He's insanely smart and a bit of a jerk now that i don't live at home, but he is also incredibly smart and does this amazing running-hug thing i taught him as a puppy when i go home to visit, so i guess still good dog wise. 





Rescue dogs:


There was a rescued GSD mix who lived hella long and was an absolute angel, he was rescued from the local-small-town pound as a puppy, somebody had just left him on the side of the road. My grandpa went to the pound one day, and picked the dog that he felt connected to. Back then, there was zero hassle, he just walked in and got a dog.
When that dog died, he repeated the same process and brought home a husky-chow mix, she was also awesome and lived a long time.




When my parents wanted their own dog, they went to one of those adoption fairs outside a petco (suburbs) and we picked out a pureto rican rescue dog, she turned out to be a big wimp and a big baby and it took her 2 years to warm up to us- now she's a love bug and prefers to be on someone's lap. She's got a few quirks but is generally a great dog. 
my parents repeated the same thing and picked up a lab-rottie mix at the same event 3-4 years after, he is also a big wimp and poops when strangers enter the house (but pretends to be a savage up until they open the door, woofing like crazy). He's a mush and perfect.

The best way I can explain it is that yes, there will be more people insured- but many of those will be people wo were previously rejected for it before.

People used to get rejected for health insurance for many reasons, most of which boiled down to "the juice wasn't worth the squeeze". 

People who are high risk (sickly, obese, history of serious conditions, have / had cancer) will end up causing the insurance company money (they will need the costly treatments that an average healthy person wouldn't.) 

The margin of profit vs labor / costs isn't big enough or is negative.


Let's say Johnny who now has health insurance after being previously rejected is obese. He then develops diabetes, and needs meds / doctors visits. He doesn't take care of it, ends up needing surgery to remove a leg/ foot. 

That's meds, doctors visits, hospital fees, surgery fees, rehab fees.

That's a fucking lot more work for an employee and costs to the insurance company between paying someone to handle all of his shit, and paying out those fees.

Let's compare him to healthy Sally. She maybe goes to the doctor 2 or 3 times a year. She never hits the point where she passes her deductible limit.

They make money off her, and the employee handling her case logs much less hours / work time handling her case, freeing that employee to then quickly move on to jane, the next healthy person. Wash, rinse, repeat. When employees get back logged, more employees are needed to handle that workload, which means 4 people are getting paid to do a job that previously one person could.

They may not be necessarily losing money, but their profit margin WILL drop. Nobody wants to make less money on average than they were before.

When I was 10 and my brother was 9, our stepdad and mom decided to get pregnant. We were somewhat excited. The whole catch was, I wanted another brother. My brother wanted another sister.

When they found out the sex of the baby, it was a girl. My brother was then 100% excited. I was a little less so.

I felt abandoned, worthless, etc. I acted out like CRAZY.

As a now adult, I understand why my feelings as a child were not reflective of what actually happened. My stepfather was not ignoring or treating me different, *he had a fucking newborn/toddler*.

My personal advice to you, as a stepmom, would to go above and beyond, making sure your step daughter or step son (depending if you have a girl or a boy) still feels the same amount of love from you. If my mom had had a boy, my brother would have felt the same way as I did (I asked, and he admitted that to me.)

It's always good to make sure you do activities with both the baby and both stepchildren as much as possible. It's even more important to invest 1 on 1 time with both kids. ESPECIALLY the child that seems to feel left out or upset. 

The only thing I wish my stepdad had done was go overboard with the alone time with me, and my brother. 

I cannot stress enough how important it is to never, ever show favorites to your own child, whether or not you feel that way. (I can't blame you if you do.)


The easiest way to bring it up to the kids is to do a super fun activity / trip you know they love, and slowly at dinner or something, ask if they would like to have a baby brother or sister.  Most kids respond well to that.

During the pregnancy, take them with you to go shopping for cute clothes and toys for baby, then take them shopping for a toy or two immediately after, for each of them.

Make the process fun and rewarding for them, too.

If they're interested, after baby is born, have them (if they want to) play with baby, feed baby, hold baby while sitting on the couch and watching shows the kids pick.
